clue.text: Natty little theatrical residence achieves comeback

indicators.note: a comeback is a return, so the assembled letters are read backwards

blocks.note: rep, short for repertory, is a little word for a theatre company
a pad is slang for one's home

explanation.surface: A smart little actor's home makes a return to fashion.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe a man who is neatly and smartly dressed, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Cover up Miss 16, creating a problem

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading the word from bottom to top

blocks.note: a lid is a cover
16 is Woodhouse, and Miss Woodhouse is Jane Austen's Emma

explanation.surface: Hushing up a scandal about some young lady causes trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cover up' reads as hushing something up, but it is a lid turned upside down in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A dilemma is a difficult choice or predicament, a synonym for a problem in everyday usage.

clue.text: Sticking out for what 8 was said to be

blocks.note: first meaning: projecting above a surface
second meaning: Mr Darcy of Pride and Prejudice was thought haughty

explanation.walkthrough: 8 points to Darcy, whose pride gives Austen's novel half its title.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both standing out from a surface and having arrogant self-regard, the charge laid against Darcy.

clue.text: Leisure reduced by kind of singular soap

definitions.note: a single character from the soap EastEnders

indicators.note: something reduced is cut short, so the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: ease is leisure or relaxation
tender means kind and gentle

explanation.surface: Free time cut short by some odd kind of soap opera.
explanation.walkthrough: EastEnders is a long-running BBC television soap set in east London; one of its characters, or any East Ender, is the singular.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking the soap's plural title and making it singular gives one Londoner from that district or one character in the show.

clue.text: Trouble with a bit of basil? More likely parsley

indicators.note: only a small piece of the following word is wanted, its opening letter

blocks.note: pother is an old word for fuss or commotion
first letter of the herb named

explanation.surface: A cook frets over a bit of basil, when parsley would suit better.
explanation.definitionFit: A pot herb is any leafy plant grown for the kitchen, and parsley is a standard example of such a culinary plant.

clue.text: Father (priest) turning up on Remembrance Day?

definitions.note: what is worn on that day, the poppy

indicators.note: in a down entry, turning upwards means the word is written from the bottom

blocks.note: papa is an old word for father
Rev, short for Reverend, is a priest's title

explanation.surface: A clergyman arrives at church for the November service of remembrance.
explanation.walkthrough: Papaver is the botanical name of the poppy, worn in Britain on Remembrance Day for the war dead.
explanation.definitionFit: The red poppy belongs to the genus of that Latin name and is the emblem pinned on lapels to mark the day.

clue.text: The wave that laid much of Mount Ida low

definitions.note: adjective: the kind of wave in 'tidal wave'

indicators.note: only a large part of the following words is used, so the answer sits inside them

blocks.note: taken from the end of Mount, all of Ida and the start of low

explanation.surface: A huge wave flattened most of the Greek mountain sacred to Zeus.
explanation.definitionFit: A tsunami is popularly called a tidal wave, so the adjective describes the type of destructive wave pictured.

clue.text: Giving teeth a nibble, Zen practitioner of Jane's ended up with ...

definitions.text: practitioner of Jane's ended up with
definitions.note: a character in Jane Austen's work who married the man in the next clue

indicators.note: something giving yields and loses its shape, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: all fifteen letters are used

explanation.surface: A Zen monk gives his teeth something to chew on, and the sentence trails into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue runs on with an ellipsis into 8: the heroine of Pride and Prejudice ended up marrying Mr Darcy.
explanation.definitionFit: Austen's heroine finishes her novel engaged to Darcy, so she is the one of Jane's people who ends up with him.

clue.text: See 6
... the sound of a bustle being heard

definitions.text: the sound of a bustle being heard

blocks.clueFragment: the sound of a bustle being heard
blocks.note: surface reading: the rustle of a Victorian dress

blocks.clueFragment: the sound of a bustle being heard
blocks.note: setter's reading: the first name of the ballerina whose surname is pronounced like that word, and also what the previous heroine ended up with

explanation.walkthrough: Continuing 6 7, Elizabeth ends up with Darcy; spelt this way it is Darcey Bussell, the British ballerina, whose surname is said like 'bustle'.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous dancer's surname sounds like that dress frame, so her first name is the one paired with the noise heard.

clue.text: Hurry up your appearance and go on and on about it

blocks.note: looks are one's appearance

blocks.clueFragment: go on and on about it
blocks.note: to harp on is to keep repeating a complaint

explanation.surface: Someone is told to hurry and smarten up, and then nagged endlessly about it.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiomatic command to move quickly, so it serves as a synonym for an instruction to hasten.

clue.text: Music presenter at pub takes spirits

blocks.note: a disc jockey presents music
an inn is a pub

explanation.surface: A radio presenter goes to the pub and orders shorts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirits' looks like whisky at the bar; here they are the supernatural beings of Arabian legend.
explanation.definitionFit: The jinn of Islamic folklore are supernatural beings, and the word is plural, so it matches spirits.

clue.text: Insect from the heart of the earth?

blocks.note: mid means the middle part
Ge, or Gaia, is the Greek goddess and personification of the earth

explanation.surface: A creature that emerges from deep underground.
explanation.definitionFit: A midge is a tiny biting fly, one particular kind of the six-legged creatures called insects.

clue.text: Riding train? Beware a poorly clad gatecrasher

indicators.note: something in poor condition is out of order, so the letters are jumbled
a gatecrasher forces a way inside, so these letters go into the middle of the other word

blocks.note: cave is Latin for beware, old school slang
taken as written
taken as written before the shuffle

explanation.surface: A warning about a scruffy intruder on a train ride.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Train' suggests the railway; here it is a long line of riders.
explanation.definitionFit: A cavalcade is a procession of people on horseback, a mounted train or retinue moving in file.

clue.text: A bad spirit: for example, "Monday shall be nameless"

indicators.note: being nameless means losing the conventional abbreviation for name, so that letter goes

blocks.note: as can mean for example, as in 'such as'
taken as written before the cut

explanation.surface: A wicked spirit is invoked, with Monday a day that dare not be named.
explanation.walkthrough: N is the standard abbreviation for name.
explanation.definitionFit: Asmoday, also Asmodeus, is a demon of Jewish legend, an evil spirit named in the Book of Tobit.

clue.text: Midland town of short story writer and misspelt humorist

blocks.note: Katherine Mansfield, the New Zealand writer of short stories
the comic novelist P G Wodehouse, with his name spelt wrongly

explanation.surface: A town in the English Midlands is linked with two famous writers.
explanation.walkthrough: The writers also chime with the theme: Mansfield Park and Emma Woodhouse are Jane Austen's.
explanation.definitionFit: Mansfield Woodhouse is a small town in Nottinghamshire, in the East Midlands of England, so it is a Midland town.

clue.text: Two lines by playwright: Anthony, or Charles II when old

definitions.text: playwright: Anthony, or Charles II when old

blocks.note: a row is a line, and a ley is a straight line linking ancient sites

explanation.surface: A list of people sharing one name, from a dramatist to a king.
explanation.walkthrough: William Rowley was a Jacobean dramatist; Anthony Rowley is the frog in the nursery song; Old Rowley was a nickname of Charles II.
explanation.definitionFit: Each named figure bore this surname or nickname: the Jacobean dramatist, the frog of the song, and the ageing king.

clue.text: See 14
Creator of chaos in a bridge

blocks.note: the article a becomes an before a vowel
an arch is a bridge or the curved span of one

explanation.surface: Someone stirring up disorder at the card table during a game of bridge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bridge' tempts thoughts of the card game; it is the structure.
explanation.definitionFit: An anarch is a poetic word for an anarchist or one who promotes lawlessness, so a maker of disorder.

clue.text: For writing a stiff note requiring the vet?

blocks.note: first meaning: a firm writing block, read as two words
second meaning: a viral disease of dogs that hardens the paw pads

explanation.walkthrough: Hardpad is a form of canine distemper, so a dog with it needs a veterinary surgeon.
explanation.definitionFit: Split in two, the word is a firm block of writing paper; whole, it names a dog disease that a vet must treat.

clue.text: Trouble about royal relative

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one word goes round the other

blocks.note: bother is trouble
R is the abbreviation for royal, as in RN

explanation.surface: A family row brews over a member of the royal family.
explanation.definitionFit: A brother is a male sibling, one kind of family member or kinsman, so he is a relative.

clue.text: Former note on short-time commission

indicators.note: short means cut down, so only a curtailed form of the next word is used

blocks.note: a breve is a long note now rarely used in music
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: An old memo about a temporary officer's appointment.
explanation.definitionFit: A brevet is a military commission promoting an officer to a higher rank without the corresponding pay.

clue.text: Give another party and retire

blocks.note: first meaning: read as ..., to stand everyone a fresh treat
second meaning: to withdraw or go back

explanation.walkthrough: The first sense splits the word into a prefix meaning again plus treat, a party or outing paid for by someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To retreat is to withdraw or fall back, so it matches retire; split, it means providing a second treat.

clue.text: Cinema detectives hold £1,000

indicators.note: to hold something is to have it inside, so one word encloses the other

blocks.note: flic is French slang for a policeman
K, short for kilo, means a thousand pounds

explanation.surface: Police officers clutching a grand at the movies.
explanation.definitionFit: The flicks is informal British slang for the cinema, from the flickering of early films.

clue.text: Maximum sentence pursued by police is what keeps them going

blocks.note: a life sentence is the longest prison term
the force is the police

explanation.surface: Chasing criminals who face life imprisonment is what motivates the police.
explanation.definitionFit: A life force is the vital energy that sustains living things, the drive that makes them carry on.

clue.text: 14 Park girl in infancy, prearranged

indicators.note: the tail of this word, arranged, means put into a new order, so the letters before it are reordered

blocks.note: a whole word plus the opening of the next, split off

explanation.surface: A girl from a stately home whose future was planned out when she was a baby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prearranged' must be split: its first three letters join the fodder and the rest is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Fanny Price is the heroine of Jane Austen's Mansfield Park, a girl taken in by her rich relatives.

clue.text: Depart from house next door to hell

blocks.note: ho is an abbreviation for house
the pit is hell

explanation.surface: Leaving a house that sits next to the inferno.
explanation.definitionFit: Hop it is a British slang command meaning go away, so it equates to depart in the imperative.

clue.text: See 23
Not carrying anything one shouldn't? Absolutely!

blocks.note: first meaning: free of drugs or weapons
second meaning: completely

explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is the adverb meaning entirely, as in clean forgot.
explanation.definitionFit: A searched suspect with nothing illicit is said to be this, and as an adverb it means utterly or completely.

clue.text: Scattered bits of deja vu in 25 exhibited by 6 7

indicators.note: only some pieces of the phrase are wanted, so the rest is dropped
things scattered are thrown about, so the kept letters are reordered
in places the jumbled letters inside the other answer

blocks.note: the answer to 25, the second half of Fanny Price
the phrase before two of its letters go

explanation.surface: Fragments of a feeling of having seen it all before, shown by Austen's heroine.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop the A and V from deja vu; the remaining four letters go between R and I.
explanation.definitionFit: Elizabeth Bennet's hasty judgement of Darcy is the prejudice of Austen's title, the fault she displays.

clue.text: Dead? Yes, possibly, and near to tears

indicators.note: possibly suggests one of several arrangements, so the letters may be reordered

blocks.note: all seven letters are used

explanation.surface: Asked whether someone has died, the answer comes with tearful eyes.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone sad-eyed has a mournful look, as if about to cry, so they seem close to weeping.

clue.text: Change sides, which is a bad thing

blocks.note: first meaning: to desert to the enemy
second meaning: a fault or flaw

explanation.walkthrough: The surface pretends to pass judgement on turncoats; the two halves are a verb and a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means abandoning one's country for another; as a noun it is a fault or imperfection.
